lesson.title: Open Circuit: When the Path Disappears
lesson.summary: An open circuit is a broken path with effectively infinite resistance, so no current can flow through it even though voltage is still present across the gap.
lesson.body:
A circuit needs a complete, unbroken loop for current to flow, the way a lap around a racetrack needs the track to be continuous. An open circuit is what happens when that loop is interrupted: a switch is flipped off, a wire snaps, a component fails, or a connector simply is not plugged in. At the point of the break, the resistance is effectively infinite, since air or empty space is an extremely poor conductor compared to copper wire. Because current depends on having a closed path, an open circuit means the current everywhere in that loop drops to exactly zero.

This connects directly back to current and resistance through Ohm's law, current equals voltage divided by resistance. As resistance approaches infinity, current approaches zero no matter how much voltage is available to push it. It is important to notice what this does not mean: an open circuit does not mean there is no voltage present, it means there is no path for charge to move. Voltage is a difference in electric potential between two points, and that difference can exist perfectly well across a gap even when nothing is flowing through it.

In fact, an open circuit produces a very specific and useful voltage reading. Since no current flows anywhere in the loop when it is open, there is no voltage drop across any of the other resistive elements in that loop, because a voltage drop across a resistor requires current through it, and here that current is zero. With zero drop everywhere else, the entire source voltage appears across the open gap itself. This is exactly what a voltmeter measures when you probe across an open switch or a broken wire, you read close to the full source voltage even though the circuit is not doing any work.

Take a simple series loop with a 9 volt battery and a 100 ohm resistor. Under normal closed operation, the current is 9 volts divided by 100 ohms, or 0.09 amps, that is 90 milliamps, and the resistor drops the full 9 volts across itself. Now suppose the switch in that loop fails open. The current immediately becomes zero everywhere in the loop. The resistor, carrying no current, drops zero volts. All 9 volts of the battery now appears across the open switch contacts, which is exactly what a technician would read with a voltmeter while diagnosing the fault.

Open circuits are not always accidents. Engineers deliberately design switches, fuses, and circuit breakers to become open circuits on purpose, interrupting current to protect equipment or to turn something off. Recognizing the signature of an open circuit, zero current everywhere in the affected loop but full source voltage sitting across the break, is one of the most common and useful diagnostic skills in troubleshooting real hardware.

A voltmeter itself is deliberately built to approximate an open circuit. Its internal resistance is designed to be extremely large, often millions of ohms, precisely so that connecting it across a component draws almost no current and therefore does not disturb the very circuit it is trying to measure. This is a direct application of the same idea, a path with near infinite resistance carries almost no current, so the meter can sit there reading a voltage without meaningfully changing the behavior of the surrounding circuit it is inserted into.
